columns.note: TanStack column defs. A `select` column (row checkbox) and an `actions` column (row menu) are NOT built in — provide them as columns when needed. A column given the id `actions` is STYLED for you: w-px, max-w-none, overflow-visible, text-clip, whitespace-nowrap. Body cells otherwise truncate at max-w-0 so long text ellipsizes, which is right for text and wrong for a column of buttons — the ellipsis there does not mean the label is too long, it means the column was squeezed and a control is half-drawn behind a "…". Naming the column `actions` is enough; meta.cellClassName is for other control columns, or to override part of what actions gets.

dataContract.rowIdentity: TanStack row.id (array index as a string) — no getRowId prop is exposed. bulkActions.onClick(selectedIds) yields these index-based ids; map to your domain ids yourself.

notes: The four had already diverged: three passed fitViewOptions padding and wc3-graph-explorer-flow did not.
proOptions.hideAttribution stays false — @xyflow/react is MIT only while the credit shows.

colorMode is derived from the `dark` class Core toggles on <html> and passed to ReactFlow, which is the only supported way to reach React Flow's own `.react-flow.dark` chrome — node fill and border, edge stroke, Controls, MiniMap. A caller can still pin a canvas by passing colorMode itself. Added when the process state machine moved onto React Flow's built-in default node, which is otherwise white with a near-black border on a near-black page.

The canvas ground is React Flow's own --xy-background-color, set to the two values reactflow.dev's example theme (xy-theme.css) uses: #f7f9fb light, #101012 dark. It replaced a bg-muted/20 class, which beat the library's own background rule; setting their variable instead leaves that rule in charge and a caller can still override through `style`. The Background dots carry no colour prop or class — the dot fill reads --xy-background-pattern-dots-color-default (#91919a / #555), never currentColor, so the text-border class that used to sit there painted nothing.

It is the ONE DOOR to @xyflow/react. Alongside the component it re-exports everything a canvas page needs — Handle, Position, MarkerType, Panel, useNodesState, useEdgesState, useReactFlow, and the Node / Edge / NodeProps / EdgeProps / Connection / FinalConnectionState types — plus the stylesheet, loaded once from here and verified to survive the tsdown build. Nothing is renamed or wrapped: these ARE React Flow's primitives, and Core-sounding aliases would only make the next person open two files to find the real documentation. What the re-export buys is that one module owns the dependency, its version and its context, so a page cannot pick up a second copy or drift onto an API this canvas has not adopted. StateMachine names no third-party package because of it; the pipeline, lineage and ontology canvases still import xyflow directly and have not been migrated.

A SELECTED node carries a 2px primary ring and a soft lift, set as React Flow's own --xy-node-boxshadow-selected rather than a rule of ours, so the library still owns when the ring appears and on which element. Its default is 0.5px of near-black, which is readable on a white node and invisible on a tinted one. React Flow scopes the declaration to the built-in node type names, so it reaches a node registered under `default` and leaves canvases with fully custom node components alone; the same rule covers :focus-visible, so a keyboard user gets the identical ring. One consequence worth knowing: because React Flow shares one variable between .selected and :focus, a node deselected by clicking it a second time keeps the ring until focus moves.

records.name: MapControlPanel
records.intent: Collapsible floating control card for a map — labelled dropdown filters over switch rows.
when: A map needs basemap, filter and layer-visibility controls in one corner
The controls must fold away so they stop covering the map

chooseOver.because: MapControls is a horizontal strip of icon buttons with a built-in geocoder and geolocate. MapControlPanel is a labelled, collapsible card for filters that need to read as named fields rather than icons.

commonMistakes: Pre-selecting every option to mean "show everything" — an empty selection is the natural "no filter", and pre-selecting 90 zones fills the trigger with noise.

Using the Select-module MultiSelect inside the panel — it renders its list as a plain absolutely-positioned element, which the card's overflow-hidden clips. The multi-select module's Popover-based MultiSelect portals out and carries the pills.
Letting the panel grow with its rows — several filters plus their pills outgrow any map. The body scrolls under `maxBodyHeight` instead.
Putting three options behind a dropdown — the click costs more than it saves. Use `as: "chips"` for short option sets and keep the dropdown for long ones.
Letting a multi-select print every pill — eight selections push the rows below it off the panel. The pills cap at four and collapse the rest into a +N popover.
Collapsing a panel to header height while keeping full width — it still occupies the surface it was meant to get out of the way of. Narrow it too.
Forcing every chip row onto one line — five options at panel width truncate to nothing. Set chipColumns and let them wrap into an even grid.
Masking a panel's scrolling body to fade its edges — that fades the content while the card's surface and border still end on a hard line. Mask the card itself.

chooseOver.because: Map is a bare basemap. ObservationsMap owns the georeferenced blueprint overlay and the observation pins, so the corner anchoring and marker lifecycle are not re-implemented per surface.

commonMistakes: Passing the four corners in an arbitrary order — Mapbox image sources require [top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left]; a rotated array renders the plan flipped or sheared.
Setting fullHeight without a height-constrained parent — `height: 100%` of an auto-height parent collapses to nothing. Give the parent h-dvh (or a flex row/column that sizes it) first.

Positioning the map container with `absolute inset-0` — mapbox-gl.css declares `.mapboxgl-map { position: relative }` and loads after the utilities, so the container is overridden and collapses to zero height. Size it with h-full/w-full instead.
Framing the blueprint when the zones are the subject — a site footprint can be an order of magnitude larger than the zones inside it, which renders them near-invisible. Pass fitTo="zones".

Feeding zone rings straight to GeoJSON — the spaces API repeats the closing point, sometimes two or three extra times. The widget collapses consecutive duplicates itself; hand-built rings should not re-add them.
Mounting a React root per observation marker to render an icon component — a busy day is hundreds of pins. The widget inlines the glyph as SVG markup (observationIcon) instead.

Setting `position` inline on a marker element — mapbox-gl.css positions `.mapboxgl-marker` absolutely, and an inline `position:relative` overrides it and drops every marker into normal document flow. Anchor a corner badge against mapbox's own positioning instead.

Guarding an overlay rebuild on `isStyleLoaded()` inside the `style.load` handler — the style does not report itself loaded yet, so the guard silently drops every custom layer on a basemap change. Reschedule on `idle` instead of bailing.
Fading a mapbox marker with `style.opacity` — mapbox-gl writes that property every render frame for terrain occlusion, so it is clobbered within a frame. Use `filter: opacity(...)` instead.

Rendering every zone in its payload colour when there are dozens — 80-plus hues compete with the status colours that actually mean something. Use zoneColorMode="neutral" and let the markers carry the meaning.

Plotting camera-detected violations as pins as well as counting them on the camera — the camera sits on their coordinates and covers them, and the badge already says how many. Keep them off the map and reachable through the camera panel.
Giving cameras a saturated colour — a camera is context, not a finding, and a bright badge competes with the status colours that carry the meaning. Keep it dark and desaturated.
Adding a zone layer without adding it to the overlay teardown — the source cannot be removed while a layer still references it, and the next rebuild throws "There is already a source with ID".
Flying back to a home view whenever the selection is empty — that fires on mount too, fighting the opening fit. Only animate on the transition out of a selection.

Animating a dash by interpolating line-dasharray — it cannot be interpolated. Step through the full fourteen-pattern cycle on a timer: the first seven only slide the dash halfway, so a truncated loop snaps back and reads as a stutter instead of travel.

Guarding paint updates on `map.isStyleLoaded()` — with a live style it stays false for long stretches while tiles load, silently skipping every update. Guard on the individual `getLayer(id)` instead; that is the condition that actually matters. (addSource/addLayer still need the style-load guard.)
Emphasising a zone selection by dimming a fill that already sits near 0.3 without also dimming its outline and label — the fill disappears while the outline and label stay, so nothing reads as faded.
Distinguishing cameras from observations by size — once both matter equally they end up the same size. Distinguish by shape: observations round, cameras square.
Hard-coding the count badge's size — it has to scale off the marker it sits on, or it swamps the badge as soon as the marker shrinks.

Binding a click handler to a map layer without excluding marker-originated events — markers sit inside the canvas container, so a marker click also fires every layer handler for whatever is underneath it. Clicking a violation would select its zone, and the map's own click would read as "clicked outside". Ignore events whose target is inside `.mapboxgl-marker`, in every such handler.

Floating a map control on its own coordinates next to a caller-supplied controls slot — it cannot know the slot's width and drifts as the slot changes. Render it inside the same row so it is laid out beside whatever is there.

Separating two colliding markers with a geographic offset — badges are a fixed pixel size, so an offset that reads at site zoom collapses when zoomed out. Test and offset in projected pixels, and re-run on zoom.
Drawing a metre radius with equal degree offsets in x and y — longitude degrees shrink with latitude, so the circle renders as an ellipse. Divide the longitude radius by cos(latitude).
Answering "is this in range" against a responder's current position when a time range is selected — they moved. Judge each item at its own timestamp, against where the responder was then.

Building a coverage corridor with buffer geometry — stroking the path at twice the radius with round caps and joins is the same shape, and needs no polygon maths. Its width is in pixels, so recompute it from metres on zoom.

Drawing a coverage corridor as a stroked line without handling a stationary responder — a short window collapses the path to one point, and a zero-length line strokes to nothing, so the coverage silently disappears. Fall back to a disc when the walked path has fewer than two distinct points.

Drawing a responder's whole window as one path — contact drops, and joining the point before a gap to the point after it invents a walk that may never have happened and claims coverage over ground nobody was on. Pass one segment per unbroken run of contact.

Faking a stationary responder's coverage with a very short line so it can share the corridor layer — mapbox drops a line below roughly a metre as too small to tile, and the coverage silently disappears with no error. Draw those runs as circle polygons.

Nudging a selected marker off a collision — its coverage is drawn at its true position, so a displaced badge sits off-centre in its own circle and reads as pointing at whatever it was nudged away from. Exempt the focused marker from de-collision.

Outlining a stationary run's disc the same way whether or not a corridor is beside it — a dashed circle at the end of an unoutlined band reads as a separate object rather than the same coverage. Outline it only when it is the whole story.

Dropping observations that arrive without coordinates — they are real reports, they just cannot be pinned. Hold them out of the map layer and list them, so the totals still reconcile and they stay reachable.
Leaving the controls corner unbounded — panels stack downward and a long list slides under the timeline. Bound the area above it and let the stack scroll instead.

Rendering a list panel only when it has rows — it then appears and disappears as the time window changes, and cannot be relied on or found. Keep it present with an empty state; "none right now" is itself worth knowing.

whenNot: Creating the process in the first place -> CreateProcessDialog
Drawing a graph nobody edits -> GraphCanvas with your own node types

chooseOver.because: GraphCanvas draws nodes and edges; it knows nothing about states, transitions or the rules between them. This carries the domain a fresh canvas would not: the four-handle node that makes self-loops and backward edges render at all, the drag guards that refuse an illegal edge during the drag, the refusal messages quoted verbatim from checkTransition(), and the cascade when a state is deleted.

The editor lived inside the Connect V3 process page and could not be mounted anywhere else. Every graph mutation routes through a pure helper and commits with one onChange(next), so the same builder serves a page, a dialog or an embed without any of them re-deriving the rules.

requiredProviders: None — GraphCanvas wraps its own ReactFlowProvider

process.note: States, transitions and the layout map. Seed one with seedProcesses() or createProcess().

onChange.note: Receives the WHOLE next record. The builder never mutates in place.

edit.note: Controlled-optional transient state — selection, last refusal, the rail add-transition draft. Pass it with onEditChange when other surfaces must agree about the selection; omit both and the builder owns it.

onNavigate.note: Opens the ontology element an inspector links to. Without it those links are plain text.

permit.note: Controlled-optional {name, type, description, policy} for the work-permit cut. `name` is mirrored onto the record through updateProcessMeta; type and description have no home on Wc3Process, so the host decides where they persist.

section.note: Which section the rail has open. Controlled-optional; ignored by variants with no shell.

onBack.note: Renders a Back button in the header band. Omitted, there is nowhere to go back to and no button is drawn.

authoring.note: This graph is being written, not inspected. Default false. Strips the header readouts (glyph, product chip, SLA badge, lint count, counts line), drops Instances and Bottlenecks from the rail, and reduces General to identity alone — no icon, no ontology binding row, none of the cards below it. One flag because they all fail for one reason: each reports on an established process, and on a graph created moments ago it is not merely empty but wrong.

formSlot.note: Fills the Form section. Defaults to a scaffold naming what belongs there.

headerActions.note: Actions for the far right of the header band — save, discard, publish. A slot rather than a prop per action, because what saving MEANS belongs to the host: a template register publishes a version, while the process page commits on every edit and has nothing to save.

railFooter.note: Extra rail cards, appended below the built-in ones. Ignored by variants with no rail.

dataContract.rowIdentity: State and transition ids are unique within one process; layout is keyed by state id.

notes: The page keeps ownership of `edit` because Instances and Bottlenecks scope off the same selection; the builder owns it when mounted alone.
variant is the declared extension axis — the node, both inspectors, the add-transition form and ProcessRailCard are exported so a variant recomposes rather than forks.
The shell moved here from wc3-process-detail.tsx so both cuts share one header and one rail; ProcessDetail is now a thin wrapper over variant=full and renders exactly what it always did.
Section order, grouping, the rule between groups and the Settings/General rename are all VARIANT_TRAITS rows, never branches in the render.

The Policy section (wc3-permit-policy.tsx) carries what a permit INHERITS from its template — validity, extensions, receiver handover, required attachments, daily sign-off and geofence. Its own module because none of it touches the graph, and it persists through the same permit value the host already owns.
Its option vocabularies (receiver eligibility, handover mode, sign-off roles) are FIXTURES; nothing in this repo models them.

Wc3ProcessState gained optional entryRequirements (action type ids collected before a permit may reach the state, on ANY incoming edge) and entryEffects (applied in order on entry). Both are optional, so no fixture needed changing.
WC3_PROCESS_EFFECTS is a FIXTURE vocabulary, not a contract — the engine's real effect set is not modelled here; only start_sla_timer is mentioned in passing. Replace it when there is a real list.

The editing rail is split State / Transition. Each tab is a LIST that expands in place — the open accordion row IS the selection, so expanding a row rings its node and clicking a node opens its row: one value, two ways to set it. Add is an in-place form under the list, not a permanently mounted card.

The canvas footer is a live validity readout, not a legend and a how-to-drag hint — both were static text that said the same thing every visit. The check is instant (processGraphLint is pure); the brief Checking state exists so a recheck is visible rather than flipping silently between two identical sentences.

The canvas is on React Flow's DEFAULTS, deliberately: the built-in default node (registered under the `default` key so the library's own node CSS applies), default bezier edges at the default #b1b1b7, default handles, default selection. It previously painted a bespoke 176x66 box - colour strip, category line, custom/proposed markers, flag row, live token pill, SLA tint - over smoothstep wiring with a stroke colour per transition kind, and read as noise beside the graphs on reactflow.dev/examples. The readouts it dropped are still on the page: the rail inspector, Instances and Bottlenecks. ONE deviation from bare default remains: each node's background is its state's identity colour mixed 14% into React Flow's --xy-node-background-color, so the canvas names a state with the same colour the rail's State list prints as a dot beside it. Mixing into the library's own node background rather than a literal white makes it land on #fff light and #1e1e1e dark from one number.

GraphCanvas is passed layout="free" so its smoothstep default does not apply: a state machine runs backwards and loops onto itself, and orthogonal segments turned every one of those into a staircase. The fit padding is passed back explicitly.

A self-loop and a backward edge take DIFFERENT handle pairs. Backward runs bottom to top and arcs under the row; a self-loop cannot, because both ends sit on one node and bottom-to-top puts all four bezier control points on the same x, drawing a straight vertical line THROUGH the node. A self-loop therefore leaves the right handle and returns into the top one, and the default curve swings clear over the top-right corner on its own.

Edges carry NO label. The transition keys are long snake_case identifiers (reject_from_submitted, reopen_from_rejected) and one on every line put more text between the nodes than inside them, crossing the neighbouring edges to do it. A transition is named in the rail's Transition list, the state inspector's outgoing rows, and the inspector an edge click opens.

The canvas is FULL-BLEED: no padded well, no gap, no Card. A rounded bordered box floating in a gutter made the canvas a picture OF the work rather than the work, and every rule around it took width the graph wanted. The editing rail is the shell's left panel mirrored — same bg-card, same one-pixel border (border-l from lg up, border-t stacked), full height, its own scroll — so the middle of the page is nothing but canvas.

Renamed from ProcessBuilder to StateMachine when the Work Permit cut landed: "process" was the wrong half of the name, because what it authors is a state machine whatever the product calls the record. The variant axis became the PRODUCT CUT — connect and work-permit — and the shell-less embed stopped being a variant, since it is not a product; it is shell={false}, which turns the rail off with it.

The two axes are deliberately separate. `variant` answers WHICH PRODUCT and today changes the left rail alone; `authoring` answers HOW OLD THE RECORD IS and strips what only an established process can report. Crossing them rather than shipping four variants is what keeps a canvas fix from being made four times — and it is why ProcessDetail takes an `isNew` prop and the Processes list tracks the id it just created in session state rather than putting a flag on the record.

Wc3ProcessTransition.actionTypeId is NULLABLE, and that is what lets a canvas drop commit. Everything else a transition needs is derived (key, kind) or came from the drag (from, to); the binding is the one field a gesture cannot supply. checkTransition no longer refuses a null binding at guard 2 — the rule moved to where it belongs, processGraphLint's L7 and the publish gate, which is the difference between 'you may not draw that' and 'that is not finished'. An unbound edge is the one place a stroke style survived the move to React Flow's defaults: dashed, because it carries state rather than decoration. L7 now has two messages for one rule, since a brand-new edge is not bound to something wrong, it is not bound yet.

The transition inspector folds actor role, guards and effects behind one button, the same call the state inspector makes about entry requirements. The Bound action type field stays above the fold alone: it is the field a drop cannot fill and therefore the field the author landed here to fill.
It keys on a hash of the graph SHAPE, not the record: every commit deep-clones the process, so keying on the record would re-check on every drag.

The tab and the add form both follow the canvas (node click, edge click, connection drop) so a gesture never fills in a hidden surface. Graph validity stays outside both tabs, being a fact about the whole graph.
SideMenuGroup gained an optional `divider` for this: unlabelled groups are otherwise separated by 2px and read as one list.
